text: To get a teardown/recreate race, force the activity to be destroyed instead of relying on timing. First check the activity's configChanges in the manifest. If it declares none, rotating to landscape or turning on dark mode destroys and recreates the activity, the preview surface and the native engine. This is faster and more reliable than timing a backgrounding against async work.

Never retry a failing automation step, recipe or diagnosis unchanged more than once. One exception: the fixture builder sometimes fails once with a transient 'new project did not open in the editor' and passes on the next try with no change, so retry it once before you rewrite the fixture steps. If something fails the same way twice, change the approach. If the fixture builder cannot reach a botto

Fire triggers and judge checkpoints from engine log lines (Msg... lines), not from fixed delays, UI timing, or analytics/UI event names. Arm the replay on a when_log engine line (for example a converted clip reaching the engine, or the engine destructor message). Then fire the lifecycle action (home, rotate) right away, or tap the next screen that still calls the engine. A fixed delay only hits so

Never guess which UI action sends an engine message, and never guess selectors, control positions or the harness API. Grep the current build to find which confirmed UI action actually sends the expected engine message, and script exactly that action. Opening and leaving a tool is often not enough, because the app may send the message only after an edit is confirmed. Gestures such as long-press dra

To make a heavy-edit ANR, an engine-thread race or a lock-contention ANR fire, try undo/redo early. Tapping the edit's apply button three times gave no main-thread ANR. Undo/redo of the same edit gave one on the first try, because it replays the full engine reload back to back while the UI posts a blocking query. The undo control (ve_btn_undo) once failed with 'not found', so confirm its selector

Control the project/draft state and the test content, and write every recipe for the draft it will actually start from. First check that the draft meets the field crash's preconditions, such as the number of clips on the target layer and special items like freezes. The default lab-phone draft has a single long clip, so split and trim checkpoints can never fire from it. Build fixture projects that

Reverse results are cached by the clip's file basename. A real reverse only runs if the item is not already reversed, its reversedUri is empty, and no file with that basename exists in cacheDir. Give fixture clips unique file names and clear the cached copy, or the reverse checkpoint never fires.

On draft open, the app re-adds saved overlays by itself about 1 s after the draft media finishes applying, using the saved path exactly as stored. Overlays added in the editor are saved as the app's own cached transcode file, which stays on disk. To reproduce a missing or broken overlay file, edit the draft so the overlay points to a separate external file, delete that file, and reopen the draft.

The harness's '--fresh on' / 'fresh app process' step only force-stops and relaunches the app. App data, SharedPreferences and open counters survive, so the app opens as an existing, already-onboarded install. Any crash that needs a first session (onboarding, first-open events, day0/openN flows) needs the recipe itself to reset the data before launching, with no permissions granted in advance.

For crashes caused by a missing Intent extra, the lab door can launch the activity directly with no extras ('launch <Activity> extras=none'). This reproduces the crash without walking the UI to the screen.

Make one attempt per app process, and make sure the old process is really gone. Start every repro cycle from a fresh process with exactly the activity stack you intend. Do not call open_draft or the open-editor/slideshow step on top of a live child screen, and do not call it again inside a recipe: the stack it leaves will not reach the teardown checkpoint. Each reopen also kills the app.

Check the installed APK before you write any recipe. The launcher name tells you nothing about the build: the lab build (developer test menu) and the Play-installed release both launch through com.myzesty/.MainActivity. Identify the build from `dumpsys package com.myzesty` (versionCode, and installerPackageName=com.android.vending for Play). Never add a setup check that aborts runs based on the la

Before writing any recipes, check that the crashing statement can actually happen in the build from this checkout. Types, nullability and callers may differ from the shipped release. If the checkout has no path that produces the faulting value, stop and report that the shipped APK is needed. Do not spend a dozen lab attempts first.

Trust the physical phone lane and plan for it to supply all the clean runs needed for repro and verify on its own. Count only that lane and treat emulator errors as noise. The emulator lane (emulator-5554) is unreliable: it once did not boot within 360 s (about 40 s when it boots at all), APK install once failed on the first try, it has been offline, and recipes recorded on the phone failed on it.

On the Android 16 lab device, opening the sticker tool right after a draft loads kills the process about 0.4 s later with am_proc_died and no Java FATAL line. Avoid that path in recipes, or the run will log a FAIL_DIED that has nothing to do with the target crash.

Treat these harness outputs as background noise, not as a crash, repro or fix-regression signal: (1) the UNDO_WITHOUT_EDITS note ('Undo became enabled with no edits'), which appears on nearly every run (including runs with no edits, engine replays and real-tap replays), has no engine aborts and does not fail the run; (2) repeated 'FD from fork' messages.

Before writing any recipe, check whether the target screen sits behind a Firebase Remote Config flag with no local override, and what value the lab phone actually gets for that flag. If the phone's config routes to a different screen, report 'needs an RC condition targeting the lab device' early instead of spending attempts on a screen that can never open.

Choose checkpoints that prove the setup, not the fault. Do not make the faulty call itself a required checkpoint (for example the call that sends the bad value): an app-side fix that stops sending it makes the checkpoint fail, and the run counts as 'trigger not reached' instead of a pass. Put checkpoints on the state that sets up the trigger (draft opened, media re-added).

Judge repro and verify runs strictly. Count a lab hit as a repro, or a crash on the fixed build as a regression, only if it is the target field crash. An ANR counts only if its main-thread frames match the field: other routes (draft open, back from a tool screen) can reach the same function and give a KeyEvent ANR with a different stack, and the 'crash on the fixed build' line can show unrelated c

A verify recipe must replay exactly the path that crashed, with real taps. Some recipes randomize per seed (leave by back key or tap, drag direction, timing), so one crashing seed does not prove the recipe is reliable: pin the recipe to the crashing path. When a crash found by a live agent is registered as a recipe, the recipe can keep only the navigation taps and drop the steps that actually trig

Make every guard (engine or app) log one distinctive line at the exact moment it fires, naming the bad value (ids, container size) and the call or state it skipped or refused. The verifier uses that line to prove each clean run reached the crash moment, which turns 'no crash' into a VERIFIED A/B result. With that line present, a run counts as clean even if a later flaky gesture checkpoint or other

Patches (fixes and repro hooks) must apply to and compile against what the lab actually builds. Lab builds swap in the field-commit versions of the files on the crash stack. Write every diff with exact line context: against the field-commit version for crash-stack files, and against the current working tree for all other files. Never write a diff from code you remember from earlier attempts.

Budget lab time realistically. An engine verify round takes about 40-45 minutes: about 1.5 minutes for the incremental arm64 build, then 2 + 6 scenario runs that each stop at about 300 s (4-5 minutes per run). A real-tap verify run takes about 3 minutes. A natural focus run with a long clip took about 225 s, so 3 repeats cost about 11 minutes. A Java/Kotlin-only fix rebuilds incrementally faster.

The root-cause self-check rejects claims that hold for only one event: timings, error order, or errors missing from other events. Such claims cost two redo rounds of about 2 minutes each. Before submitting, check that every timing, error and step in the trigger is present in every event, and keep single-event claims out of the main story.

For use-after-teardown or null-object crashes, fix it once at the shared getter, or make the owner live for the whole process. This matters most when many JNI entry points reach the null owner. A guard that only makes the faulting function return a default value (0, empty, null, or a thrown exception) often just moves the crash. Be especially wary of a native guard that throws.

For an out-of-range index crash, unlike a use-after-teardown crash, a bounds guard at the crash site is the right engine fix. Reject exactly the out-of-range inputs: an invalid outer index, and an inner index past the container size. The reviewer checks that the guard covers every index the loop reads, so state that coverage in the fix. This passed the critic and code review on the first round.

Fix both levels in the first proposal. If the engine crashed because the app sent a wrong call (such as a stale index or id from a Kotlin screen's own copy of a list), the proposal must contain the Kotlin fix as the real fix, with the engine guard only as hardening. An engine-guard-only patch passed the lab but was blocked by code review in every round as not fixing the real cause. Grep all caller

For an ANR where the main thread sits in a blocking engine Get/GetResult call, do not only harden the wait. First look for a Java/Kotlin caller that polls the engine in a loop on the main thread with no exit condition or timeout. Hardening only the engine promise path failed the lab twice, because that loop kept issuing new blocking calls. The proposer gate also rejects a diff that only adds a tim

Overlay tool in PlayerActivity: the Overlay tab (ve_tab_overlay) is about the 10th item in the horizontal bottom bar and is off-screen on the phone, so scroll the bar before you look it up. In a draft that already has overlays, the tool does not open the gallery picker, so don't wait for gallery-only ids like deselect_button; select an existing overlay instead. A recipe module must define every lane function the harness asks for (<name>_a(ed, r) and <name>_b(ed, r)). Selectors must use the harness syntax, for example 'id:...'. Bare names like 'mediaList' are rejected before anything runs.
